Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) process was chosen to begin with for metal-polymer composite manufacturing as LPBF offers better precision in fabricating thin struts. Triangular lattice was chosen due to its high strength. The process settings used for fabricating this triangular lattice structure were a laser power of 130W, beam speed of 1500 mm/s, 45 m layer thickness, and 50 m hatch spacing. The laser powder bed system printing metallic lattice and the machined metal lattice fitted into the mold are shown in Fig. 3.2.1(a). Next, binder jet process was chosen for fabricating the metal lattice specimens due to its cost effectiveness when produced industrially. The limitation with the binder jetting however is difficulty in printing very thin features and thus the strut thickness needs to be increased. Using 316L Stainless Steel infiltrated with bronze, several tensile and shear specimens were fabricated to perform mechanical testing on the lattice designs and evaluate their efficacy. The process setting used in the binder jetting process are a layer thickness of 100 m, 1 g/ml binder density, 60% powder packing rate. The printed binder jet tensile and shear specimens placed in the compression mold are depicted in Fig. 3.2.1(b). The details of base material properties obtained via mechanical testing and surface roughness measurement for the binder jet printed samples are investigated and elaborated in Section 5.2. In the first subsection, the CF/PA66 overmolding on triangular metal lattice within 6” x 6” mold is described. The polymer composite preforms printed in BAAM is heated within the mold during the overmolding. However, for the preforms of larger size (14” x 14”) preforms are heated separately prior to placing in the mold and compression. Due to this slight variation in the manufacturing process, the overmolding of larger preforms is included in a separate subsection. 3.3.1 Overmolding in small (6” x 6”) mold The triangular metal lattice is first placed within the 6” x 6” mold and the CF/PA66 preform cut into square plaque to fit exactly within the mold is placed on top as shown in Fig. 3.3.1 (a) & (b), respectively. The mold was heated up to 2400 C and a pressure of 6.434 MPa was applied for 5 minutes while the temperature is maintained at 2400 C. Subsequently, the heat was turned off and the system was cooled down at room temperature and under 6.434 MPa pressure for 25 minutes to obtain the hybrid metal polymer composite panel shown in Fig. 3.3.1(c).
